elements.name: Time-Triggered Architecture
elements.what: System-level organization in which all communication and computation are driven by the progression of a fault-tolerant global time base, with statically planned activation instants known a priori at all nodes.
elements.problem: Distributed hard real-time systems need temporal predictability, composability, and fault isolation; event-driven activation makes worst-case behavior and certification arguments hard, while a global static schedule makes temporal behavior verifiable by construction.
elements.named_in: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

elements.name: Event-Triggered Architecture
elements.what: System-level organization in which communication and task activation are initiated by the occurrence of significant events (interrupts, message arrivals) rather than by a global clock; Kopetz names it as the counterpoint to time-triggered control.
elements.problem: Sporadic, low-rate, or unpredictable stimuli waste bandwidth and CPU under static time-triggered schedules; event triggering gives flexibility and responsiveness at the cost of harder worst-case analysis and possible event showers.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

elements.name: Temporal Firewall
elements.what: A unidirectional, time-controlled shared-memory interface between subsystems: the sender deposits temporally accurate state data that the receiver reads at predefined instants, with no control signals crossing the interface in either direction.
elements.problem: Control-flow coupling (interrupts, handshakes) lets timing faults propagate between subsystems; a data-only interface with a priori known access instants blocks error propagation and makes each side independently analyzable.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

elements.name: Fault Containment Region
elements.what: A set of components (typically a node computer) engineered so that the immediate consequences of an internal fault stay inside the region's boundary, which is defined and enforced architecturally.
elements.problem: Without designated containment boundaries a single fault can corrupt arbitrary parts of a distributed system, defeating redundancy; partitioning the system into independent FCRs is the precondition for any fault-tolerance argument.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

elements.name: Fault-Tolerant Unit
elements.what: A group of replica-deterministic fault containment regions that produce the same outputs so that the failure of a member is masked by the remaining replicas (duplex fail-silent or triplicated voting configurations).
elements.problem: Individual nodes fail; grouping FCRs into an FTU lets the architecture deliver correct service despite the failure of any single member without involving the application.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

elements.name: Time-Triggered Bus
elements.what: A broadcast communication channel whose access is governed by a static TDMA schedule: each node owns pre-assigned slots in a cyclic schedule known to all nodes, so message timing is known a priori.
elements.problem: Contention-based buses make message latency load-dependent and unbounded in the worst case; a static slot schedule gives constant, verifiable latency and doubles as a fault-isolation mechanism (babbling nodes are cut off by bus guardians).
elements.named_in: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

elements.name: Time and Space Partitioning
elements.what: An operating-system-enforced structure in which applications run in partitions with statically allocated memory regions (space) and fixed cyclic execution windows (time), so no partition can affect another's resources or timing.
elements.problem: Hosting multiple applications of different criticality on one computer risks interference; enforced partitioning lets mixed-criticality software share hardware while preserving the independence that certification requires.
elements.named_in: ARINC 653 - Avionics Application Standard Software Interface - AEEC (living)

elements.name: Integrated Modular Avionics
elements.what: A domain reference architecture in which multiple avionics functions, formerly on dedicated boxes, are hosted as partitioned applications on a shared set of common computing modules with standardized interfaces (ARINC 653 APEX) and defined supplier roles.
elements.problem: Federated one-function-one-computer designs multiply size, weight, power, and spares; IMA consolidates functions onto shared platforms while preserving per-function independence through robust partitioning and incremental certification.
elements.named_in: DO-297 - Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) Development Guidance and Certification Considerations - RTCA (2005)

elements.name: Federated Avionics Architecture
elements.what: The traditional avionics system structure in which each function runs on its own dedicated computer with private resources, integrated only through inter-box data buses.
elements.problem: Physical separation gives inherent fault containment and simple per-box certification, at the cost of hardware proliferation; it is the named baseline against which IMA and partitioned architectures are defined.
elements.named_in: DO-297 - Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) Development Guidance and Certification Considerations - RTCA (2005)
elements.borderline: Named mostly as the contrast concept to IMA; kept because avionics sources name it as an architecture in its own right and dedicated-hardware design elements need a specific bridge endpoint.

elements.name: Health Monitor (ARINC 653)
elements.what: A standardized architectural function that detects and reports faults at process, partition, and module level and applies configured recovery actions (restart, stop, switch) per level, defined by configuration tables rather than application code.
elements.problem: In a partitioned system, error handling must itself be partition-aware and criticality-aware; a system-level, table-driven monitor keeps fault escalation and recovery policy out of individual applications and under certification control.
elements.named_in: ARINC 653 - Avionics Application Standard Software Interface - AEEC (living)

elements.name: AUTOSAR Layered Software Architecture
elements.what: The automotive reference layering for ECU software: application layer above the RTE, above basic software split into services, ECU abstraction, and microcontroller abstraction (MCAL) layers, plus complex device drivers as a sanctioned bypass.
elements.problem: Automotive software must be portable across ECUs and suppliers; a standardized layer stack with fixed interface contracts decouples application components from hardware and lets OEMs integrate multi-vendor code.
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Classic Platform - Layered Software Architecture - AUTOSAR (living)

elements.name: AUTOSAR Virtual Function Bus / RTE
elements.what: A communication abstraction in which software components interact through typed ports on a virtual bus, generated per-ECU as the runtime environment (RTE) that maps port communication to intra-ECU calls or network signals.
elements.problem: Component-to-component communication must be independent of deployment; the VFB lets components be designed against logical connections and relocated across ECUs, with the generated RTE realizing each mapping.
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Classic Platform - Layered Software Architecture - AUTOSAR (living)

elements.name: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform
elements.what: The POSIX-based automotive reference architecture for high-performance ECUs: dynamically scheduled applications communicate via service-oriented ara::com middleware (SOME/IP) instead of the Classic platform's static signal routing.
elements.problem: Autonomous-driving and connectivity functions need dynamic deployment, high compute, and update-over-the-air, which the statically configured Classic platform cannot provide; the Adaptive platform standardizes a service-oriented alternative alongside it.
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform - Explanation of Adaptive and Classic Platform Software Architectural Decisions - AUTOSAR (living)

elements.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer (architectural layer)
elements.what: A dedicated layer in the firmware stack that presents hardware-independent interfaces for all peripheral and processor access, so every layer above it is portable across boards and silicon.
elements.problem: Direct register access scattered through application code welds the product to one chip; concentrating hardware knowledge in one boundary layer makes ports, test doubles, and vendor changes tractable.
elements.named_in: Reusable Firmware Development: A Practical Approach to APIs, HALs and Drivers - Beningo (2017)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm catalogs hardware-abstraction-layer as an API-shape mechanism; this entry is the layer as a position in the system's layer stack (parked from Phase 1, admitted here).

elements.name: Board Support Package
elements.what: The packaging of all board-specific software - boot code, clock and pin configuration, device drivers, memory maps - into one named unit that adapts an OS or firmware stack to a particular hardware board.
elements.problem: An OS or product firmware must run on many boards; isolating everything board-specific into a replaceable package makes 'support a new board' a bounded, well-understood unit of work.
elements.named_in: Mastering Embedded Linux Programming, 3rd ed. - Simmonds (2021)

elements.name: Superloop Architecture
elements.what: A whole-system structure with no operating system: one endless main loop polls and services every task in turn, optionally with interrupts as the foreground layer feeding flags/buffers to the background loop.
elements.problem: Small systems cannot afford an RTOS's footprint and complexity; a single statically ordered loop gives minimal overhead and full determinism of structure, at the cost of coarse timing control and poor scalability.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's super-loop is the loop mechanism itself; sources (Pont SUPER LOOP, Simon's Round-Robin in his 'Survey of Software Architectures' chapter) also treat it as the system-architecture choice against RTOS-based structure - that architecture sense is this entry.

elements.name: Function-Queue-Scheduling Architecture
elements.what: A system structure in which interrupts enqueue pointers to task functions and the main loop dequeues and runs them to completion, allowing priority ordering of the queue without a preemptive kernel.
elements.problem: Round-robin loops cannot prioritize urgent work and full RTOS preemption may be overkill; queueing work as functions gives priority control and bounded response with cooperative simplicity.
elements.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)

elements.name: RTOS-Based Architecture
elements.what: A whole-system structure in which the application is decomposed into prioritized, preemptively scheduled RTOS tasks communicating through kernel objects (queues, semaphores, events), with response times set by priority rather than loop position.
elements.problem: When response requirements differ by orders of magnitude across activities, cooperative loops cannot bound latency for the urgent ones; a preemptive kernel decouples each activity's worst-case response from the rest of the system.
elements.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)

elements.name: Bootloader-Application Split
elements.what: Partitioning firmware into a small, rarely-changed bootloader image and one or more application images in separate flash regions, with the bootloader validating, selecting, updating, and jumping to the application.
elements.problem: Field-updatable devices must survive a failed or interrupted update; keeping an immutable boot stage that can verify images and fall back (golden image, A/B banks) makes the update path recoverable and the root of trust small.
elements.named_in: From Zero to main() series - Memfault Interrupt (2019)

elements.name: Safety Executive
elements.what: A centralized component that tracks safety-relevant events and coordinates all shutdown, recovery, and fail-safe transitions for the system, separating safety policy from the functional channels it supervises.
elements.problem: When safety measures are scattered across subsystems, complex shutdown sequences and cross-subsystem fault policy become inconsistent and unverifiable; centralizing them in one executive makes the safety logic auditable.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Monitor-Actuator
elements.what: A two-channel structure separating the actuation channel from an independent monitoring channel that checks the actuator's physical effect against setpoints and forces a fail-safe state on divergence.
elements.problem: A single channel that both acts and checks itself shares failure modes between the two duties; an independent monitor with its own sensing detects actuation-channel faults without doubling the actuation hardware.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Channel Architecture
elements.what: Organizing the system as one or more end-to-end channels, each a sequential chain of data transformations from sensing to actuation, so that redundancy and safety measures can be applied per-channel.
elements.problem: Safety and reliability engineering needs a unit to replicate, diversify, or protect; structuring the system as identifiable channels creates that unit and localizes data flow for analysis.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Homogeneous Redundancy
elements.what: Replicating identical copies of a channel or component (in space or in time) and switching or comparing between them to survive random hardware faults.
elements.problem: Random hardware failures take down single channels; identical replicas restore service cheaply in design effort - but by construction cannot catch systematic (design) faults common to all copies.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Heterogeneous Redundancy
elements.what: Providing redundant channels that are deliberately different in design or implementation (different hardware, algorithms, or teams) so that a systematic fault in one channel is unlikely to be replicated in the others.
elements.problem: Identical replicas share design faults; diversity buys protection against systematic errors at the cost of developing and qualifying multiple distinct channels.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Triple Modular Redundancy
elements.what: Three identical channels compute in parallel and a voter forwards the majority result, masking any single channel failure without interruption of service.
elements.problem: Fail-over redundancy has a detection-and-switch gap; majority voting removes the gap by masking the fault instantly, at the price of triple resources plus a voter that becomes the critical element.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: MooN Voting Architecture
elements.what: The safety-instrumented channel topologies named MooN in IEC 61508: N channels of which M must agree/demand for the safety function to act (1oo1, 1oo2, 2oo2, 2oo3, 1oo2D...), each with defined diagnostic and voting arrangements.
elements.problem: Safe-failure and dangerous-failure probabilities pull channel topology in opposite directions (spurious trips vs missed demands); the MooN family names the standard trade-off points and the standard's SIL tables quantify them.
elements.named_in: IEC 61508:2010 - Functional safety of E/E/PE safety-related systems - IEC (2010)

elements.name: Watchdog (architecture pattern)
elements.what: A system-level supervision structure: an independent watchdog component (often on separate hardware with its own time base) receives liveness/sanity evidence from the supervised channels and initiates recovery or fail-safe shutdown when evidence stops or fails checks.
elements.problem: A hung or corrupted system cannot rescue itself from within; placing the last-resort monitor outside the supervised computation, with an independent clock, keeps recovery credible under common-mode failure.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's watchdog is the timer mechanism and its kick discipline; Douglass's RTDP Watchdog Pattern is the system-level supervision structure cataloged here.

elements.name: Dual-Core Lockstep
elements.what: Two identical processor cores execute the same instruction stream cycle-aligned (one delayed a few cycles) while comparators check their outputs every cycle, signaling a fault on any divergence.
elements.problem: Software-visible redundancy cannot catch transient hardware faults inside the CPU with low latency; cycle-level comparison of redundant cores detects them immediately and transparently to software, at the cost of doubled silicon.
elements.named_in: Cortex-R5 and Cortex-R5F Technical Reference Manual - Arm (2011)
elements.borderline: Hardware-adjacent: the structure lives in silicon, but it is a named system-architecture option that safety firmware is designed around (fault response, self-test hooks) and a bridge endpoint for error-detection design elements; distinct from the design realm's deterministic-lockstep (game networking).

rejected.name: Sparse global time base
rejected.why: Kopetz names it, but it is a property/model of the time domain underpinning TTA, not a structural element; TTA's entry carries the concept.

rejected.name: Fail-silent unit
rejected.why: Kopetz's fail-silence is a failure-mode assumption placed on an FCR, not a separate structure; noted in the FCR/FTU entries.

rejected.name: MCAL / ECU Abstraction Layer / Complex Device Driver
rejected.why: Named sub-layers of the AUTOSAR layer stack; splitting them out would fragment one reference layering into non-bridgeable shards.

rejected.name: APEX API
rejected.why: The ARINC 653 partition API is the interface of the partitioning architecture, not a separate architecture element.

rejected.name: Cyclic executive (architecture sense)
rejected.why: The design realm's cyclic-executive already carries the timeline/major-minor-frame vocabulary; at system level the choice it represents is covered by the superloop and time-triggered style entries. Flag for the editor: if Phase 3b needs a distinct avionics-style cyclic-executive endpoint (Baker & Shaw 1989), it can be split back out.

rejected.name: Round-Robin with Interrupts (Simon) / foreground-background system
rejected.why: Simon distinguishes it from plain round-robin, but Labrosse and common usage equate foreground/background with the superloop family; kept as aka to avoid over-splitting one bare-metal style.

rejected.name: Safety island
rejected.why: Real SoC construct (Arm/NVIDIA automotive platforms) but naming is vendor-doc level and hardware-platform scoped; establishedness as a software-architecture element too thin this pass.

rejected.name: Limp-home / degraded mode operation
rejected.why: Parked by embedded-mech, but it is the graceful-degradation family - resilience-scout territory (Graceful Degradation is on the parked list under that scout); dropping here to avoid cross-scout duplication, not from the catalog.

rejected.name: Subsumption architecture / Sense-Plan-Act (robotics)
rejected.why: Established robotics reference architectures (Brooks 1986; Murphy) but outside this charter's corpus base; flagged as a gap-sweep candidate if no scout owns robotics/CPS control structures.

rejected.name: Models of computation (synchronous-reactive, SDF, discrete-event - Lee & Seshia)
rejected.why: Named and canonical (leeseshia) but they are architecture-description/semantic-model constructs (kind: description) closer to an ADL/MoC scout's territory; flagged as thin spot rather than claimed here.

rejected.name: OSEK/AUTOSAR OS conformance classes (BCC/ECC)
rejected.why: API conformance profiles of an OS standard, not architectural structures.

rejected.name: Triple Core Lock-Step (TCLS)
rejected.why: Arm's TCLS (2016/2019 papers) is the voting variant of core lockstep; folded as aka.

notes: 28 elements, charter band 18-32. Parked items from p3/parked.json ingested here: HAL, BSP, TTA, ARINC 653 time/space partitioning, AUTOSAR layered architecture, AUTOSAR VFB/RTE, bootloader split, safety executive, monitor-actuator, channel architecture, homogeneous/heterogeneous redundancy, TMR, dual-channel-at-system-level (as MooN voting, the more specific IEC 61508 naming - design realm already owns dual-channel/protected-single-channel), lockstep. NOT taken (other scouts' territory per parked-list attribution): microkernel, layered pattern (POSA1), event-driven architecture, active-object framework, five-layer architecture (RTDP douglass-samek generic layers), hierarchical control, recursive containment, virtual machine pattern, ROOM/component-based, data bus, broker, client-server, limp-home/graceful degradation, SOA generic. Same-name-two-realms handled with -arch/-architecture suffixed ids for HAL, superloop, watchdog; design-realm collisions checked against elements_index.txt (super-loop, watchdog, hardware-abstraction-layer, dual-channel, protected-single-channel, n-version-programming, cyclic-executive, deterministic-lockstep, time-triggered-co-operative-scheduler, schedule-table). Pass-8 addendum candidates cited with named_in_corpus_id=null: RTCA DO-297 (2005; verified live - GlobalSpec/Wikipedia/FAA AC 20-170 confirm title and federated-vs-IMA usage) and Arm Cortex-R5/R5F TRM (2011; verified live - developer.arm.com DDI 0460 documents DCLS). Simon's dsimonprimer 'Survey of Software Architectures' chapter grounds the superloop/function-queue/RTOS style triad. Thin spots: models of computation (leeseshia) and robotics control architectures (subsumption, SPA) are unclaimed if no other scout covers them; sensor-fusion/CPS control-loop structures from wolf5/marwedel yielded no crisply named architecture elements beyond what is here.
